CERT-In — cyber defence controls for MSMEs
Google Ads — Customer Match policy

title: How to choose a franchise consultant for your brand
excerpt: Compare development partners through scope, deliverables, fees, relevant evidence and the responsibilities that remain with your team.
introHighlight: Choose a franchise consultant by the work your business needs and the evidence that the proposed team can deliver it. A consultant may help develop the model, prepare materials or support recruitment, but those are different services. Define the assignment before comparing proposals.

sections.heading: Diagnose the work you need
body: List the decisions that remain unresolved: readiness, unit economics, format design, operating manuals, commercial structure, recruitment or support systems. Decide which capabilities already exist internally and which require external help. A business with an untested operating model needs different assistance from a developed brand seeking qualified partners. Avoid buying a broad growth package simply because it sounds comprehensive. The first useful conversation should clarify the problem and identify work that may need legal, accounting or sector specialists.

sections.heading: Ask for concrete deliverables
body: Request a scope showing outputs, inputs required from your team, responsible people and review milestones. A promise to develop the franchise should be translated into specific work, such as a documented format, cost model or recruitment process. Clarify whether implementation, training and revisions are included. Ask to see appropriately shared examples of relevant work without requesting another client’s confidential information. Evaluate whether the proposed deliverables will be usable by your operating team after the engagement ends.

sections.heading: Review evidence and the delivery team
body: Ask who will perform the work, what experience is relevant and how specialist questions are handled. Request references with suitable permission and ask about the actual scope delivered. A list of logos or claimed introductions does not establish the quality of development work. Be cautious about guarantees of franchise sales, rapid expansion or fixed returns. A credible proposal should recognise the business’s evidence gaps and explain how they will be investigated rather than promise certainty before assessment.

sections.heading: Understand fees and potential conflicts
body: Compare fixed fees, staged payments, retainers and success-based charges with the precise deliverables and triggers. Ask who else pays the adviser, including brands, suppliers or referral partners, and how potential conflicts are managed. Clarify ownership and permitted use of completed materials, confidentiality, termination and unfinished work. Obtain legal review of the engagement where appropriate. A low headline fee can be misleading if necessary activities or revisions are excluded, while a higher fee still needs a clear basis.

sections.heading: Set a review and handover process
body: Agree how progress will be evaluated and how your team will approve or challenge outputs. Keep assumptions and unresolved questions visible. The consultant should not replace management’s responsibility for the business or specialist advice outside the engagement’s competence. Plan the handover of files, working models, contacts and operating knowledge. A useful engagement leaves the brand better able to make and execute decisions, rather than permanently dependent on an adviser whose method or records it cannot access.

faqs.q: Should I choose a consultant who guarantees franchise sales?
faqs.a: Treat such a guarantee cautiously and examine its exact terms and evidence. Recruitment outcomes depend on the offer, market, candidate fit and execution; a promise should not replace a credible development and assessment process.

faqs.q: Is a success fee better than a fixed fee?
faqs.a: Neither is universally better. Compare incentives, deliverables, triggers and exclusions. Understand whether the adviser is rewarded for suitable long-term relationships or only for an early transaction.

sources.label: India Code — Indian Contract Act, 1872
WIPO — intellectual property and franchising
US Federal Trade Commission — franchise evaluation questions; US disclosure rules are not Indian law

title: Resolving franchise disagreements before they escalate
excerpt: Create a fair process for documenting issues, clarifying responsibilities and selecting the appropriate resolution route.
introHighlight: A franchise disagreement should be handled through a clear process that separates facts, operating fixes and legal questions. Early discussion can help, but serious disputes may need specialist advice. The objective is an accurate understanding and an appropriate resolution, not pressure to avoid every formal complaint.

sections.heading: Define the issue in specific terms
body: Record what each side says happened, the relevant dates and the documents or commitments involved. Separate a service problem from a disagreement about contractual rights. For example, a delayed supplier delivery may need an immediate operating solution while a dispute over mandatory purchasing needs a different review. Avoid labels about motive or character. A factual record helps the people involved identify the actual point of disagreement instead of arguing across several unrelated concerns.

sections.heading: Address urgent operating consequences
body: Identify any immediate risk to customers, staff, data or continuity and use the appropriate response process. Do not wait for a commercial dispute to be settled before addressing a safety concern. Preserve relevant records securely and obtain competent advice where necessary. Temporary arrangements should be documented and should not casually imply a permanent change in rights. The practical aim is to prevent further harm while the underlying issue is investigated through the correct channel.

sections.heading: Use accountable internal escalation
body: Give the partner a named route to raise the concern and explain who will review it. Avoid sending them repeatedly between sales, operations and finance. Set a realistic response process and identify missing information. Where the person reviewing the issue made the disputed decision, consider an additional reviewer. Keep communications professional and record material discussions. A workable escalation process makes concerns easier to examine without promising that every request will be accepted.

sections.heading: Consider the appropriate resolution route
body: Review the agreement and obtain legal advice about the available options. Negotiation or mediation may be suitable for some disagreements, while others require a different process. WIPO describes mediation as a facilitated process rather than an imposed decision; its suitability depends on the dispute and parties. Do not assume an informal discussion replaces required contractual notices or legal deadlines. The resolution route should be chosen deliberately, with an understanding of costs, confidentiality and authority to agree terms.

sections.heading: Document and learn from the outcome
body: Record what was agreed, who will act and how completion will be checked. Have material settlement or contractual changes reviewed appropriately. Clarify whether the outcome is specific to one case or changes a wider policy. Examine whether unclear documents, inconsistent promises or weak support created the problem. Share relevant process learning without exposing unnecessary sensitive information. A resolved disagreement can improve the system, but only if the cause is addressed rather than filed away as an isolated difficult relationship.

faqs.q: Should every disagreement go straight to legal action?
faqs.a: No. The appropriate route depends on the issue, urgency, agreement and advice. Some matters can be resolved through documented discussion, while others require prompt specialist or formal action.

faqs.q: Does mediation guarantee a settlement?
faqs.a: No. It can help parties explore a resolution, but an outcome is not assured. Review whether the process is appropriate and who has authority to agree any resulting terms.

sources.label: WIPO — mediation questions and procedures
India Code — Indian Contract Act, 1872

title: Standardising financial reports across franchise outlets
excerpt: Use consistent definitions and reconciled records to understand outlet performance without confusing sales, profit and cash.
introHighlight: A network financial report should make comparable information visible while preserving differences in format and local costs. It needs consistent definitions, reliable records and a clear purpose. A dashboard cannot compensate for inconsistent treatment of revenue, expenses or cash movements at the outlet.

sections.heading: Define the decisions the report supports
body: Identify whether the report is used for royalty reconciliation, operating support, planning or another agreed purpose. Collect information proportionate to that purpose and consistent with the agreement. Avoid asking for every possible financial field because the system allows it. Separate the needs of the outlet owner from the central team’s oversight. A focused report is more likely to be maintained accurately and can make discussions about costs, staffing or stock more practical.

sections.heading: Agree definitions and categories
body: Define sales, refunds, discounts, direct costs, payroll, occupancy and franchise charges consistently. Explain how online settlements, vouchers and transfers are treated. Work with an accountant on appropriate reporting and tax considerations; this is a management-reporting framework, not a prescribed accounting treatment. Provide examples of ambiguous transactions. If one outlet records a delivery-platform deduction as reduced sales and another as an expense, apparent comparisons can be misleading even when both totals reconcile locally.

sections.heading: Reconcile before comparing
body: Connect reported figures to relevant point-of-sale, bank, stock and accounting records. Investigate unexplained differences rather than smoothing them away to meet a reporting deadline. Keep a process for corrections and version history. Distinguish estimates from closed-period figures. A late but clearly identified adjustment is more useful than a silent change that makes earlier decisions impossible to understand. Assign the outlet and central responsibilities so neither assumes the other has checked the underlying data.

sections.heading: Read profit and cash separately
body: A profitable period can still require cash for inventory, deposits, debt payments or delayed settlements. Show the relevant cash timing alongside operating performance. Compare outlets with similar formats and conditions, and explain material differences in rent, staffing or trading age. Avoid using a network average as a guaranteed target. The report should help ask better questions about performance, not declare one partner weak merely because their circumstances differ from the most successful location.

sections.heading: Turn the report into a working review
body: Use a short review to identify significant changes, causes and actions. Check whether a cost increase reflects price, quantity, waste or recording. Agree who will investigate unresolved items and when. Protect access to commercial information and avoid unnecessary circulation across the network. Review whether each requested field is still useful. Financial reporting adds value when it supports a practical decision and a traceable follow-up, rather than becoming a monthly exercise in uploading numbers nobody discusses.

faqs.q: Can sales reports replace accounting records?
faqs.a: No. Sales data is one input. Accounting, bank, stock and other relevant records are needed to understand expenses, obligations and cash flow accurately.

faqs.q: Should every franchisee’s detailed results be shared with the network?
faqs.a: Not automatically. Review confidentiality, permission and the purpose of sharing. Aggregated comparisons can be useful where they are appropriate and do not misrepresent differences between outlets.

sources.label: US Small Business Administration — business management guidance; US legal details do not apply to India
RASCI — retail occupational responsibilities

title: Supporting an underperforming franchise outlet
excerpt: Diagnose the causes of weak performance and agree a realistic recovery plan without promising a turnaround.
introHighlight: Underperformance needs a diagnosis before a remedy. Low sales, weak margins and cash pressure are different problems and may occur together. Review reliable evidence with the operator, identify what can be changed and agree a time-bound plan without guaranteeing recovery.

sections.heading: Establish what is below plan
body: Compare actual results with the assumptions used for the outlet, considering trading age, season and local conditions. Separate revenue, contribution, operating expenses and cash needs. Check the records before drawing conclusions. A stock-recording error can distort margin, while a delayed settlement can create cash pressure without changing sales. Define the problem in measurable terms so the support discussion does not become a general statement that the outlet needs to work harder.

sections.heading: Investigate the main causes
body: Examine customer demand, access, offer, staffing, service, stock and local marketing. Observe the operation and speak with the manager. Look for evidence that distinguishes a temporary issue from a structural mismatch. Avoid assuming that more advertising will solve every problem. Increased demand can worsen complaints if service capacity is already weak. Consider the brand’s own role in site approval, training or supply rather than treating every disappointing result as the franchisee’s failure.

sections.heading: Choose a manageable set of actions
body: Prioritise changes that address the identified cause and can be implemented with available resources. Assign owners and define the expected evidence of progress. A service problem may need training or scheduling; excess stock may need a purchasing review. Obtain specialist financial or legal advice where the situation involves debt, contractual changes or potential insolvency. Do not recommend additional investment simply to preserve the original forecast without reassessing the business case and risks.

sections.heading: Set review points and limits
body: Agree when the plan will be reviewed and what would justify continuing, changing or stopping a particular action. Monitor cash needs and urgent obligations closely with appropriate professional support. Keep concessions or temporary changes documented through the correct process. A recovery plan should not become an indefinite sequence of small extensions with no evidence of improvement. Be honest about uncertainty and the possibility that the original format or site may not be viable under current conditions.

sections.heading: Capture lessons for the wider network
body: Review whether the issue reveals a weakness in recruitment, site assessment, opening costs or support. Improve the relevant process for future outlets. Share learning appropriately without exposing the operator’s confidential information. If exit or restructuring becomes necessary, use professional advice and the contractual process rather than improvising. The brand’s responsibility is to provide the support it has committed to and a serious evidence-based review, not to promise that every location can be turned around.

faqs.q: Should marketing spend be increased first?
faqs.a: Only if evidence shows that awareness or acquisition is the relevant constraint and the outlet can serve additional demand. Investigate operations, margin and cash before assuming more promotion is the answer.

faqs.q: How long should a recovery plan run?
faqs.a: Use the trading cycle, available cash and nature of the actions to set realistic review points. There is no universal period, and urgent financial or legal concerns need appropriate specialist attention.

sources.label: US Small Business Administration — business management guidance; US legal details do not apply to India
ISO — quality assurance and process design

title: Assessing whether a franchise partner is ready for multiple outlets
excerpt: Review management depth, cash planning and operating controls before awarding additional locations to an existing partner.
introHighlight: Running one outlet well is useful evidence, but multiple locations require a different management structure. Assess the partner’s ability to supervise through people and systems rather than personal presence alone. Additional rights should follow a documented review of capability, funding and support needs.

sections.heading: Examine how the first outlet succeeds
body: Identify whether performance depends on the owner being present for every difficult decision. Review the manager’s capability, staff stability, records and customer issues. Strong results achieved through unsustainable personal hours may not transfer to a second location. Look beyond revenue and check whether routines remain reliable during absence. The question is whether the operating system is strong enough to support another unit, not whether the owner is enthusiastic or has identified an attractive new site.

sections.heading: Review the management structure
body: Ask who will supervise each outlet and how the partner will receive accurate information. Define the role of an area manager or other support where needed. Check recruitment and training capacity before promising a rapid opening sequence. A second outlet can expose gaps previously covered informally by the owner. The brand should understand the proposed delegation and escalation arrangements, including how serious issues will be handled when several locations need attention at the same time.

sections.heading: Assess funding across the group
body: Review the capital and operating cash required for the next location without assuming the first outlet can fund it immediately. Consider the effect of shared staff, inventory and debt obligations with appropriate financial advice. Keep outlet-level performance visible so one location’s cash does not conceal another’s problem. Ask how slower openings or simultaneous cost pressures would be handled. Additional expansion should not depend on optimistic transfers of cash that have not been tested in the plan.

sections.heading: Use a staged development approach
body: Link future openings to evidence such as trained management, reliable reporting, adequate funding and acceptable operating standards. Review the relevant agreements and development obligations with counsel. Avoid awarding a large area solely as a reward for good personal relationships. Clarify what happens if a site is not approved or a milestone is delayed. A staged process can preserve opportunity while giving both sides evidence before larger commitments accumulate.

sections.heading: Monitor the transition after expansion
body: Review whether the partner’s time, support requests and outlet performance change after the second location opens. Look for hidden dependence on the brand’s field team or an overextended manager. Adjust support and development plans through the appropriate process. Use the findings to improve future multi-unit assessments. The aim is a capable operating group with clear accountability, not simply a higher outlet count attached to one partner’s name.

faqs.q: Should strong sales automatically qualify a partner for another outlet?
faqs.a: No. Review management depth, controls, funding and consistency as well as sales. The first outlet may depend on circumstances that will not transfer.

faqs.q: Is a dedicated area manager always required?
faqs.a: The need depends on outlet complexity, geography and the partner’s role. What matters is a credible management and escalation structure with enough capacity to supervise each location.

sources.label: RASCI — retail occupational responsibilities
US Small Business Administration — business management guidance; US legal details do not apply to India

title: Planning franchise renewal before the agreement ends
excerpt: Review the contractual timetable, operating record and future investment early enough for both sides to make an informed decision.
introHighlight: A renewal review should begin early enough to examine the agreement, outstanding obligations and future operating plan. Renewal is not something to assume from a good relationship. The available rights, conditions and notice requirements depend on the actual contract and applicable law.

sections.heading: Start with the contractual timetable
body: Have the relevant agreement and amendments reviewed to identify the term, renewal provisions, notice process and conditions. Record important dates and responsible people. Do not substitute an internal policy for the rights actually granted. If the wording is unclear, seek legal advice before making commitments. The review should allow time for discussion and independent advice rather than creating last-minute pressure because the expiry date was not tracked.

sections.heading: Assess the operating relationship
body: Review standards, reporting, payments, support delivery and unresolved issues using factual records. Include the brand’s performance as well as the partner’s. Distinguish an isolated problem from a continuing pattern and give the operator a clear opportunity to discuss findings. Renewal should not become a surprise presentation of old complaints that were never raised through the agreed process. Keep commercial negotiation separate from any formal response to alleged contractual breach.

sections.heading: Evaluate the next operating period
body: Review the format, market, premises and investment needed to continue. Identify likely equipment replacement, refurbishment or system changes and who would fund them. Check the lease and other dependencies alongside the franchise term. A renewed brand agreement may be impractical if the premises arrangement ends earlier or major costs have not been assessed. Financial assumptions should be updated using current evidence and reviewed appropriately rather than simply extending the original business plan.

sections.heading: Explain proposed terms and changes
body: Set out any proposed fee, support, territory or operating changes clearly, subject to the existing rights and legal review. Give the partner a usable comparison and time to consider it. Avoid suggesting that every change is routine merely because the document is called a renewal. Record agreed exceptions and unresolved questions. The final documents should match the commercial understanding, with no reliance on informal promises that the next operating team may not know about.

sections.heading: Plan either continuation or transition
body: If renewal proceeds, complete the documentation and update systems, support plans and relevant records. If it does not, use the agreed exit process and appropriate professional advice. Consider customers, staff, open orders, brand assets and outstanding obligations. A respectful, organised transition protects service continuity and reduces avoidable conflict. The renewal process should produce a clear decision with enough time to implement it, rather than leaving both sides uncertain until the final trading period.

faqs.q: Is renewal automatic after a successful term?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Review the actual renewal rights and conditions in the agreement, along with applicable law. Do not rely solely on verbal expectations.

faqs.q: Should refurbishment be discussed only after renewal?
faqs.a: No. Identify material future investment early enough for the partner to evaluate the commitment. Review how any requirement is authorised and documented under the actual arrangement.

sources.label: India Code — Indian Contract Act, 1872
US Federal Trade Commission — franchise evaluation questions; US disclosure rules are not Indian law

title: Managing a franchise exit and brand handover
excerpt: Plan customer continuity, records, digital access and brand removal through the agreed process when a franchise relationship ends.
introHighlight: A franchise exit needs a coordinated plan for the obligations that remain after trading or brand use changes. Follow the agreement and obtain appropriate legal advice. The process should protect customers and records while clarifying access, outstanding payments and the use of brand assets.

sections.heading: Establish the agreed exit position
body: Review the reason, timing and legal basis for the exit, including relevant notices, amendments and outstanding disputes. Identify who is authorised to coordinate the process. Do not assume that a decision to stop trading immediately resolves every obligation. Preserve necessary records and seek specialist advice on matters such as employees, creditors, leases or regulated services. An operational checklist supports the process but cannot replace the legal review of the actual circumstances.

sections.heading: Map unfinished customer obligations
body: List open orders, prepaid services, returns, warranties and complaints. Determine who will communicate with customers and how legitimate obligations will be fulfilled or addressed. Keep personal information protected and share it only through an appropriate process. A change of operator or brand can be confusing, so customer messages should accurately explain what is happening. Avoid promises about refunds or continued service until the responsible parties and practical arrangements have been confirmed.

sections.heading: Control physical and digital brand assets
body: Identify signage, packaging, uniforms, manuals, websites, profiles, domains and advertising accounts affected by the exit. Review ownership and permitted use under the agreement and relevant platform rules. Plan removal, transfer or updating in the proper sequence. Do not rely on a verbal instruction to delete everything. Some records may need preservation, and abrupt account changes can disrupt legitimate customer communication. Keep an accountable record of actions and unresolved access issues.

sections.heading: Reconcile stock, equipment and money
body: Check the agreed treatment of remaining stock, deposits, credits, loans, equipment and supplier commitments. Verify quantities and condition where a return or transfer is proposed. Document the calculation and supporting evidence for final settlements. Obtain accounting and legal advice on the actual treatment. A general statement that all dues are cleared should not replace a review of relevant records or resolve issues that the parties have not actually agreed.

sections.heading: Complete and review the handover
body: Use a completion record showing what was done, what remains and who owns the next step. Remove unnecessary system access while preserving required information securely. Confirm the responsible contact for any later customer or commercial issue. Review the causes of avoidable friction and improve future agreements, onboarding or support where appropriate. An orderly exit does not mean every disagreement disappears, but it gives the parties a clear operational record instead of leaving critical tasks to assumption.

faqs.q: Should all customer data be deleted on the exit date?
faqs.a: Not automatically. Review ownership, purpose, privacy requirements and legal preservation obligations. Use an agreed, documented process for transfer, retention or deletion with appropriate advice.

faqs.q: Can the former outlet keep using the brand temporarily?
faqs.a: That depends on the rights and permissions actually agreed. Do not assume continued use is allowed. Obtain clear legal and commercial guidance and document any authorised transition arrangement.

CERT-In — cyber defence controls for MSMEs

title: How to scale a service business through franchising
excerpt: Standardise delivery, scheduling and accountability for service networks where the work extends beyond a storefront.
introHighlight: A service business becomes more transferable when its delivery process is defined, teachable and measurable across locations. The challenge is often the work between booking and completion. A franchise model should explain that process and its economics, rather than relying only on a recognisable name and lead-generation promise.

sections.heading: Map the complete service journey
body: Trace enquiry, quotation, booking, dispatch, delivery, approval, payment and after-service support. Identify where the customer’s property, premises or information is involved. A laundry collection network, home-repair service and training business have different handovers, but each needs clear accountability. Record who performs the work and who resolves a failure. If a central facility or subcontractor is involved, include that relationship in the model rather than presenting the franchisee as controlling steps it cannot actually manage.

sections.heading: Define the unit of work
body: Choose a useful unit for planning, such as a completed job, collection route, service appointment or batch. Estimate the labour, travel, materials and rework associated with it. Distinguish a booking from a completed paid service. Model practical capacity, including preparation and gaps between jobs. A service network can appear busy while producing weak contribution if travel is scattered or repeat visits are common. Use observed operating evidence before presenting the format as readily scalable.

sections.heading: Standardise judgement and escalation
body: Document the decisions staff can make, the information required and when a specialist must be involved. Not every service can be reduced to a fixed script. Identify the qualifications and experience needed for more complex work and review applicable requirements for the activity and state. Train staff to recognise the limits of their role. The customer should receive a dependable process for quotations, changes and complaints rather than a different explanation from every technician or outlet.

sections.heading: Build local delivery capability
body: Assess recruitment, training, scheduling, equipment and supply needs in the target market. A flow of central leads does not create qualified staff or transport capacity. Test how the outlet handles absence, cancellations and urgent rework. NSWS can provide indicative approval guidance, but the actual service requires its own local and sector review. Pilot the handoffs and reporting before expanding widely so the brand understands the support burden created by the operating model.

sections.heading: Use quality and repeat demand to guide expansion
body: Track completion, rework, complaints, contribution and repeat customers together. National Consumer Helpline guidance provides useful context for clear information and redress, while the brand must implement a practical service process. Review whether the model works without constant founder intervention and whether local partners can deliver consistently. Expand in manageable stages with defined support. Service franchising is strongest when the brand can demonstrate how work is fulfilled reliably, not merely how enquiries are generated.

faqs.q: Can a strong lead-generation system make a service franchise ready?
faqs.a: It helps only if the business can fulfil the resulting work reliably and economically. Assess staffing, scheduling, quality, customer handling and support before treating demand generation as a complete model.

faqs.q: Should every service use the same operating manual?
faqs.a: Core policies may be shared, but task-specific skills, equipment, customer risks and local requirements need appropriate instructions. Avoid forcing materially different services into one generic workflow.
